facts.statement: Titanichthys is an extinct genus of giant marine placoderms found in the shallow seas of the Late Devonian in Morocco, Eastern North America, and possibly Europe.
facts.quote: Titanichthys (meaning "titanic fish") is an extinct genus of giant, aberrant marine placoderm from shallow seas of the Late Devonian of Morocco, Eastern North America, and possibly Europe.

facts.statement: Titanichthys is assumed to have been a filter feeder that used its large mouth to swallow schools of small fish or zooplankton, retaining prey with its mouth-plates while expelling water.
facts.quote: It is assumed that Titanichthys was a filter feeder that used its capacious mouth to swallow or inhale schools of small, anchovy-like fish, or possibly krill-like zooplankton, and that the mouth-plates retained the prey while allowing the water to escape as it closed its mouth.

facts.statement: Titanichthys is considered the first known large-sized vertebrate filter feeder, with jaws functionally similar to those of baleen whales and basking sharks.
facts.quote: A study has since confirmed this assumption as its jaws are functionally closer to that of filter feeders like baleen whales and basking sharks, and it appears to have developed from benthic durophagists that became pelagic suspension feeders. This would make it the first (known) large-sized vertebrate filter feeder.

facts.statement: While Titanichthys was once estimated to reach 7 to 7.6 meters in length, a 2023 study by Engelman suggests it was likely comparable to Dunkleosteus, measuring about 4.1 meters.
facts.quote: Titanichthys was estimated to have reached a length of 7 - 7.6 m, but Engelman (2023) suggested that Titanichthys was comparable in size to Dunkleosteus, likely measuring about or just over 4.1 m in length.

facts.statement: Titanichthys is classified as a basal aspinothoracid, most closely related to the genera Bungartius and Tafilalichthys.
facts.quote: Titanichthys is thought to have been a basal aspinothoracid, closest related to Bungartius and Tafilalichthys.

facts.statement: When geologist Henri Termier first found fossils of Titanichthys termieri, he initially placed them in the genus Gorgonichthys before convincing colleagues they belonged to a placoderm rather than a dinosaur.
facts.quote: When the first fossils of T. termieri were found by geologist Henri Termier, the specimens were originally placed within the genus Gorgonichthys - that is, after Termier was able to convince his colleagues that the bone scraps were of a placoderm, and not a dinosaur.

facts.statement: Titanichthys lived during the Eifelian to Famennian stages, approximately 393.47 to 358.86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Eifelian to Famennian (393.47 to 358.86 million years ago)
